abstract:
The development of category theory in univalent foundations and the formalization thereof is an active field of research. Categories in that setting are often assumed to be univalent which means that identities and isomorphisms of objects coincide. One consequence hereof is that equivalences and identities coincide for univalent categories and that structure on univalent categories transfers along equivalences. However, constructions such as the Kleisli category, the Karoubi envelope, and the tripos-to-topos construction, do not necessarily give univalent categories. To deal with that problem, one uses the Rezk completion, which completes a category into a univalent one. However, to use the Rezk completion when considering categories with structure, one also needs to show that the Rezk completion inherits the structure from the original category.
In this work, we present a modular framework for lifting the Rezk completion from categories to categories with structure. We demonstrate the modularity of our framework by lifting the Rezk completion from categories to elementary topoi in manageable steps.

 1      Introduction
Univalent foundations [23] has proven itself to be an adequate foundation for the development
of mathematics and category theory in particular. In univalent foundations, structures adhere
to the principle that equality and equivalence of structures coincide, such that equivalent
structures are indistinguishable. This principle is known as the univalence principle [5].
    For structured sets, such as monoids or groups, posets, or setoids, this principle is usually
a consequence of the univalence axiom, which postulates that principle for types. That is,
both equivalence (i.e., isomorphism) and equality between such structured sets coincide with
equivalence and equality, respectively, on the underlying sets. However, for higher-dimensional
structures, such as categories, the story is more subtle [2, 23]. For categories to adhere
to this principle, we need an equivalence between the identity type (A = C) and the type
(A ≃ C) of adjoint equivalences. The univalence axiom implies that we have an equivalence

      between (A = C) and the type of isomorphisms (A ∼       = C). Hence, the univalence principle
      for categories can be restated as having an equivalence (A ∼  = C) ≃(1) (A ≃ C). However, (1)
      does not hold in general, unless when we consider univalent categories: categories for which
      identity and isomorphism for objects are equivalent.
           The univalence condition for categories is met by many naturally occurring categories
      in UF. This condition can furthermore be motivated by looking at the set-theoretic models
      of UF, such as Voevodsky’s simplicial set model of homotopy type theory [14]. In this
      model, types are interpreted as simplicial sets, and so the interpretation of categories (in
      HoTT) gives rise to a bisimplicial set which is a Segal space. Specifically, one simplicial set
      interprets the objects (and the internal homotopies or identities), and the other interprets the
      morphisms, and both are connected by source, target, and identity maps of simplicial sets.
      Under this interpretation, the univalence condition corresponds precisely to the completeness
      condition for Segal spaces. Observe, however, that we do not obtain all Segal spaces, due
      to the set condition on the hom-types in HoTT. Hence, (univalent) categories in HoTT
      correspond to truncated or 1-categorical (complete) Segal spaces, whose higher homotopies
      on the morphisms are trivial.
           Even though univalence for categories is, by the aforementioned reasons, a “natural”
      condition, different constructions do not produce univalent categories; see Section 2. This is
      where the Rezk completion comes into play.
           Abstractly, the Rezk completion refers to the univalent completion of a category [2]. That
      is, the Rezk completion of a category C is a univalent category RC(C), together with a functor
          ηC
      C −→ RC(C), which satisfies the following universal property. For every univalent category E,
      any functor of type C → E factors uniquely through ηC . Ahrens et al. [2] proved that this
      universal property is equivalent to the requirement that ηC is a weak equivalence. However,
      the weakness of this equivalence means that ηC need not have an inverse. In particular,
      structure on C is not guaranteed to transport across ηC to a structure on RC(C).
           In this work, we present a modular approach to lift the Rezk completion from categories
      to structured categories, such as elementary topoi. In particular, we show that the Rezk
      completion of a topos inherits the structure of a topos and that the universal property
      extends to the level of topoi. Furthermore, this work is accompanied by a formalization in
      the Rocq-library UniMath, and our approach is designed with this formalization in mind. In
      particular, our approach is modular and is designed to be applicable to a lot of structures a
      category can have. Furthermore, we expect our approach to be practical for the formalization
      hereof in any proof assistant based on homotopy type theory.

      1.1    Prior Work
      As for (1-)categories, higher-dimensional categories are supposed to satisfy an additional
      univalence condition such that they adhere to the univalence principle. A general theory
      making this precise has been developed by Ahrens et al. [5] where a signature for finite-
      dimensional categorical structures has been developed and a notion of equivalence has
      been formulated for such structures, which for e.g. categories coincides with the notion of
      equivalence.
          Different categorical theories have been developed in univalent foundations, including
      the theory of monoidal categories [33], enriched categories [25], bicategories [1], and double
      (bi)categories [28, 20]. In particular, those works formulated the notion of univalence for
      such categorical structures, which coincide with the one given by Ahrens et al. [5].
          The Rezk completion [2] has been lifted to multiple categorical structures, including some
      of the mentioned above [1, 33, 25]. Furthermore, the Rezk completion has been constructed
      for a class of structured groupoids [30].

    Moreover, univalent category theory, and the Rezk completion in particular, has been
used in the study of denotational semantics. For instance, the Rezk completion is used to
construct from a category with representable maps of presheaves a univalent category with
families [4]. Furthermore, the Rezk completion is used to relate two different constructions
of Scott’s representation theorem, which model the untyped λ-calculus [24]. Lastly, various
classes of topoi and their internal logic, based on comprehension categories, are constructed
in the univalent setting by Van der Weide [27].


1.2    Overview and Contributions
This paper is structured as follows:
1. Section 2 contains background material on univalent categories and the Rezk completion.
2. In Section 3, we discuss the framework and strategy for lifting the Rezk completion from
   categories to structured categories. We start by briefly recalling some of the basics of
   displayed bicategories. Then we define the notion of displayed universal arrows as an
   intermediate step for the modular construction of biadjoints. Afterwards, we discuss how
   such arrows specialize in the case of lifting the Rezk completion.
3. In Section 4, we apply the framework presented in Section 3 to lift the Rezk completion
   from categories to various classes of structured categories where we work our way up
   to W-topoi. More precisely, we consider finitely (co)complete categories (Section 4.1),
   cartesian closed closed categories (Section 4.2), elementary topoi (Section 4.3), and
   W-topoi (Section 4.4).
4. In Sections 5 and 6, we elaborate on the different methods to extend the Rezk completion
   to categories with structure found in the literature and possible ways in which this work
   can be extended.


1.3    Formalization and Foundations
This work is accompanied by formalization in the Rocq-library UniMath on univalent math-
ematics [22, 31]. The logic underlying the UniMath library is an intensional dependent type
theory whose universes satisfy the univalence axiom. We do not rely on the axiom of choice,
except in Lemma 39, nor the law of excluded middle. We rely on propositional truncation.
   The formalization, and this work, makes heavily use of the already existing material
on (bi)category theory in the UniMath-library and the accompanied literature [2, 1]. The

 2     On the Rezk Completion for Categories

In this section, we recall and elaborate on the Rezk completion for categories. Most of the
material in this section is already found in the original paper on univalent categories [2].
First, we recall the definition of univalent categories in Definition 2. Then we recall weak
equivalences (Definition 3) and we recall the Rezk completion in terms of weak equivalences
(Definition 5). Afterwards, we zoom in on some examples of categorical constructions where
the Rezk completion plays a role. Lastly, we discuss a bicategorical formulation of the Rezk
completion, which we use in Sections 3 and 4 to lift the Rezk completion from categories to
structured categories.

      Univalent Categories. In univalent foundations, categories C consist in particular of
      a type of objects ob(C) and for every pair of objects x, y : ob(C) a type of morphisms
      C(x, y). Furthermore, a category C consists of a composition operation on the morphisms

      is associative and unital. Lastly, each C(x, y) is a set, which means that equalities between
      morphisms form a proposition; recall that a type A is a proposition if each identity type
      x = y is equivalent to the unit type, for every x, y : A.

Examples. We now discuss some examples and constructions of categories to illustrate
the following aspects concerning the Rezk completion. Example 7 illustrates that the Rezk
completion generalizes certain constructions on set-theoretic structures such as groups and
posets. Examples 8 and 9 illustrate that working in univalent foundations distinguishes
constructions which are classically equivalent. Example 10 is the motivating example of this
work, where we have a construction of topoi which usually does not produce a univalent
topos. Hence, to construct an alternative univalent construction thereof, the Rezk completion
is essential. In particular, Example 10 illustrates that we need sufficient results about the
transfer of structure from a category to its Rezk completion. Of course, this observation also
plays a role in the other examples.

      ▶ Example 7 (Setcategories). A setcategory is a category whose type of objects is a set.
      Often, such categories are not univalent.
      1. The walking iso category, i.e., the category with two distinct but isomorphic objects, is
         not univalent. The Rezk completion hereof is the terminal category. More generally, we
         can consider a set with a preorder, which is equivalently a setcategory whose hom-sets are
         propositions. Such a category is univalent if and only if the preorder is anti-symmetric [2,
         Exa. 3.14] Hence, the Rezk completion of a preorder is its posetal completion.
      2. A monoid M is equivalently a one-object setcategory BM . If M contains more than
         one invertible element, this category is not univalent. If M is an abelian group, the
         Rezk completion of BM is the Eilenberg-MacLane space of M [16, 7], which in univalent
         foundations can be constructed via higher inductive types. In particular, whereas the
         Rezk completion for preordered sets can be understood as picking out a representative
         of every equivalence class, this example illustrates that non-trivial identities are added.
         Furthermore, η : BM → RC(BM ) is an example of a weak equivalence that does not
         have an inverse.
      3. The Rezk completion allows for the construction of quotients of sets. Indeed, let A be a
         set equipped with an equivalence relation ≃ (i.e., a setoid). Then A can be made into a

         a ∼ b. This makes A into a groupoid. The Rezk completion for A is then a groupoid
         whose objects are equivalence classes of ∼. More generally, the Rezk completion can be
         seen as a generalization of the groupoid quotient [30].

A bicategorical perspective. To lift the Rezk completion from categories to structured
categories, we formulate the Rezk completion bicategorically.

3.1    Displayed Bicategories and Structured Categories
In the remainder of this paper, we make heavy use of displayed bicategories, and we start
by recalling this notion. Displayed bicategories serve various purposes, and one of these
is that we can use them to modularly construct bicategories and to modularly prove their
univalence [1, 3]. To understand what displayed bicategories are, let us first recall an
example of a displayed category. We can construct the category Mon of monoids and monoid
homomorphisms by endowing the objects and morphisms of Set with extra structure and
properties. Specifically, for every set there is a type of monoid structures on it, and for
every function between sets with monoid structures on them we have a type expressing
that this function is a homomorphism. One must also prove that the identity function is a
homomorphism and that homomorphisms are closed under composition. Displayed categories
generalize such descriptions of categories. Specifically, in a displayed category D over a
category C, we have a type D(x) of displayed objects over every object x : C and a set x̄ →f ȳ
of displayed morphisms for every morphism f : x → y and displayed objects x̄ : D(x) and
ȳ : D(y). Displayed bicategories generalize displayed categories to the bicategorical setting.
     The bicategories we consider have as their 2-cells just the natural transformations – i.e.,
each type of 2-cells is contractible. That is, we require no compatibility conditions between
the natural transformations and the additional structure. This contractibility assumption
is often met when considering categories equipped with structures defined via universal
properties, such as finitely complete categories, cartesian closed categories, and elementary
topoi. This assumption, in turn, offers a lot of simplifications when stating definitions and
verifying properties. For example, the definition of a displayed bicategory reduces to the
following, and is thus a simplified version as compared to [1].

        5     Related Work
       We elaborate on the different methods to extend the Rezk completion to categories with
       structure found in the literature.
           Ahrens et al. [4] extended the Rezk completion to categories with families (CwFs).
       That is, they showed that every weak equivalence into a univalent category (i.e., the Rezk
       completion) induces a map from the type of CwFs on the domain to the type of CwFs on the
       codomain. Furthermore, they constructed for every weak equivalence an equivalence between
       the representable map structures on the involved categories. These results allowed them
       to construct an equivalence between representable maps of presheaves on a category and
       the CwFs on its Rezk completion. While our focus has been on displayed bicategories with
       contractible 2-cells, CwFs and representable maps require propositional 2-cells. Nonetheless,
       Theorem 25 could be slightly generalized to have propositional 2-cells. In particular, we
       expect our methodology to also work for these structures.
           Veltri and Van der Weide [30] proved that the inclusion of the bicategory of univalent
       groupoids into the bicategory of all groupoids admits a left biadjoint. Furthermore, it was
       shown that this biadjoint lifts to a variety of structures on groupoids. However, instead
       of considering each structure individually, as we have done, they presented a signature for
       higher inductive types to encode structure on groupoids and they showed that the inclusion
       of structured univalent groupoids into structured groupoids admits a left biadjoint. In
       particular, they considered algebraic structure, whereas we consider structure defined via
       a universal property. Furthermore, while we work with biadjoints in terms of equivalences
       between hom-categories, they worked with biadjoints in terms of the unit-counit description.
           Wullaert et al. [33] extended the Rezk completion to monoidal categories. In particular,
       they also proved that the biadjoint given by the Rezk completion lifts from categories
       to monoidal categories, although not in the exact same words. The approach considered

 6     Conclusion

Conclusion. We presented a modular approach for lifting the Rezk completion from cat-
egories to structured categories, based on displayed universal arrows (Definition 23). We
illustrated this approach, and its modularity, by lifting the Rezk completion from categories to
topoi (Corollary 52). In particular, we’ve observed that the lifting of the Rezk completion es-
sentially reduces to the preservation and reflection properties of weak equivalences. Moreover,
the approach presented here is independent of an explicit construction, but follows from its
characterization in terms of weak equivalences. However, while elementary topoi already
illustrate that various structures do lift, Lemma 39 illustrates that for certain structures
we need additional assumptions in our logical foundation. Lastly, topoi are an important
notion in categorical logic and semantics since they allow for an interpretation of various type
formers and logical constructs. Hence, our results imply that the Rezk completion preserves
these operations, which means that the Rezk completion can be used for the construction of
univalent models.


Future Directions. There are multiple ways in which this work can be extended. First,
in [1, Constr. 5.13], it is proven that the presheaf construction for the Rezk completion of
(1-)categories induces a similar result when passing to (locally univalent) bicategories. Hence,
there is the question of how the results presented here generalize to higher categories and
topoi (see e. g. , [21, 32]).
    Second, our results imply that the tripos-to-topos construction (Example 10) can be
extended to a tripos-to-univalent-topos construction. Consequently, this can be used for the
construction of realizability topoi. Specifically, if we start with a realizability topos, our
results imply that its Rezk completion is topos. However, it remains to be seen whether
the Rezk completion is itself a realizability topos, i.e., by verifying that it satisfies the
assumptions that characterize realizability topoi axiomatically ([10, Thm. 4.6]).
